message.content:
**ATP synthase (Complex V) in mitochondria** | Feature | Description | |---------|-------------| | **Location** | Inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae). | | **Structure** | • **F₀ subunit** – a proton‑conducting channel embedded in the membrane.
• **F₁ subunit** – a soluble catalytic domain protruding into the matrix. | | **Primary Function** | **Synthesis of ATP from ADP + inorganic phosphate (Pi)** driven by the proton motive force (ΔpH + ΔΨ) generated by the electron transport chain. | | **Mechanism** | 1. Protons flow back into the matrix through F₀, causing rotation of the c‑ring.
2. Rotation induces conformational changes in the β‑subunits of F₁, sequentially binding ADP & Pi, catalyzing their condensation into ATP, and releasing ATP.
3. The process is highly efficient: ~3 ATP molecules per full rotation. | | **Energy Source** | The electrochemical proton gradient (Δp) created by Complexes I–IV. | | **Biological Significance** | • Provides the bulk of cellular ATP (~90 % of total production).
• Couples oxidative phosphorylation to metabolic demand.
• Essential for energy‑dependent processes (muscle contraction, ion transport, biosynthesis). | In short, ATP synthase converts the energy stored in the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane into chemical energy stored in ATP, making it the central enzyme of cellular respiration.
